title: Pauri 26, meaning: priceless
hookLine: priceless His virtues and His dealings; many have described Him and gone on describing (Japji 26)

cards: Ask what someone would carry out of a burning house, and it's rarely the TV. It's a grandfather's photo, a child's first shoes, a cheap ring that belonged to someone.
Put any of those up for sale online and they're worth almost nothing. Try to take them away and they're worth everything. The price tag and the value have nothing to do with each other.
Pauri 26 takes that feeling, applies it to everything, and then asks who could ever describe it.

teach.b: Amul: a, not; mul, price. Priceless. Not expensive, which still has a number.
Beyond numbers altogether. Pauri 26 stamps it on everything. In paraphrase: priceless the virtues and the trade, the traders and the storehouses.
Priceless those who come, priceless what they carry away. Priceless the love, and priceless those absorbed in it.
Priceless the law and the court, the scales and the weights, the blessings and the signs of grace, the command itself.
Then, in the original: amulo amul aakhiaa na jaae. Priceless beyond priceless, it can't be told. Then a long, wide turn.
Many describe it, the stanza says, in paraphrase. The Vedas and the Puranas; the learned, with their commentaries. Brahmas and Indras.
The gopis and Govind. Shiva, and the siddhas.
Gods and demons, humans, sages and servants. So many have described it and gone on describing, have spoken and risen and left. If as many again were made, they still couldn't tell it.
Notice who's in that list: scriptures, gods and sages from the world Guru Nanak lived in.

All are honored as describers, and all fall short, because the thing is amul. It's as great as it wishes to be, and only the True One knows. So the lesson reaches all the way down to a pair of child's shoes.
The most valuable things don't have a price. They're not less real for that. They're more.

how: Pauri 26 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs hear its long list of describers, from the Vedas to the gods and sages, as a reminder that no one can fully tell the worth of the One.

o: rare, found in only a few places
without any price, beyond being measured
very costly, worth a great deal of money

games.q: what's inside Pauri 26 — tap the pairs.

s: it means without price: beyond numbers altogether.
Pauri 26 names the Vedas, gods and sages as describers
all are honored as describers, and all fall short.
Pauri 26 mocks the gods and scriptures it names
none is mocked; the thing described is simply amul.

games.q: the Vedas, the gods, the sages have all tried to describe the One. what does Pauri 26 say if as many again were made?
o: they would argue with each other.
games.why: so many have described it and gone on describing; if as many again were made, they still couldn't tell it. it's amul.

practice: Choose one ordinary thing near you: a cup, your own hand, the chair, the light through the window.

Look at it as if it were priceless and couldn't be replaced: its shape, its color, what it does for you, who made it, how long it has served. Let it be amul for a while, then close your eyes and rest.

wordCard.voice: Amul. Priceless: a, not, and mul, price. Pauri 26 says it of every virtue and every dealing, and says no describer, however great, can tell it all.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: amul, priceless; a (not) + mul (price). Japji Pauri 26 repeats it line after line.

carryVoice: Your line: priceless, all of it. Even the Vedas fell short of telling it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 5–6 (Japji, Pauri 26, the priceless lines and the describers)
